utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Today is Wednesday, and I'd like to greet everyone here in the courtroom, the Prosecution, the Defence and the accused, as well as all of you assisting us here in this courtroom. I believe that Mr. Scott wants to take the floor, but before I give him the opportunity to speak, I'd like to remind you that the Prosecution filed a motion for -- to add four exhibits to the 65 ter list, and that's in relation to Witness Bo Pellnas. The Defence is expected to respond to the motion filed by the Prosecution, and because this is quite urgent since we are expecting this witness next week, the Trial Chamber has decided to set as tomorrow, 2.00 p.m., the deadline for the Defence to respond. If at 2.00 p.m. we have not received any responses from the Defence, we'll issue our decision. That will be very quickly filed, officially filed, with the registry. Let's now talk about the time remaining for the witness today. A number of calculations have been made, and it appears that the Defence has one hour and 42 minutes left, and -- including one hour for Mr. Praljak, and 25 minutes for the Defence of Mr. Petkovic. I understand that Mr. Scott wanted to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, Mr. President, and to the other Judges, Judge Trechsel, Judge Prandler, good afternoon, and to all those in the courtroom. I wanted to raise a topic and I felt based on the way that the time has progressed yesterday and given the estimates that the president just indicated, that time wouldn't be such a pressing issue today. It's always seemingly an issue of some sort but perhaps we have a bit more time today than we often have. And before we continue with this witness, Your Honour, I wanted to address a couple of points, two separate points. The first is this, and it may impact the remainder of the examination of this witness, which is another reason I want to raise it now. It seems to the Prosecution that recently again, and including much of yesterday, that a great deal of Defence time in cross-examination time is being devoted to what the Prosecution submits is essentially tu quoque. The Muslims did this. There were these atrocities at Uzdol, there were these atrocities at Doljani. There were all these -- that sort of thing. Now, let me put my comments very clearly in context and what the Prosecution's position is in this case so that it's not misunderstood. Your Honour, I personally, as long ago as the opening statement in this case, if anyone can remember back in April, at the end of April 2006, said the Prosecution does not dispute, has never disputed, and will not dispute that in this terrible war that we've all come to know a bit about there were bad actors on every side; Croat, Muslim, and Serb. And there were victims on every side; Croat, Muslim, and Serb. And as a personal statement, my heart and my sympathy, and I'm sure the Prosecution teams and I'm sure many on the Defence, if not all the Defence, goes out to the victims on all sides. The Croat victims, Muslim victims, Serb victims. Indeed I would go further and just say, and again for the record and to put my comments in context, there's only, with all respect, one organisation in the courtroom that investigates, charges, and prosecutes crimes within the jurisdiction of this Tribunal committed or allegedly, let me say allegedly, to be a good lawyer, by Muslims, and that is the Office of the Prosecutor, and indeed, if I can say, our own, our very own Mr. Mundis is about to lead the Prosecution in the Delic case, an alleged Muslim perpetrator. We are well aware and have never disputed that crimes and atrocities and terrible things were committed by Muslims in this horrible conflict and that there were Croat victims in this horrible conflict. None of that is disputed. It will not be disputed. Now, having said all that, much of what's been put to witnesses, much of the time that's been spent on these matters is completely irrelevant as a defence. A long time ago it was clearly established that tu quoque is not a defence, and in the wisdom of international law one party cannot say, it's okay if we did it because the other side did it too. They all did it, and, for that matter, a pox on all their houses, Croat, Muslim, or Serb. It is not a defence or relevant to any issue unless something -- something very specific is articulated that provides a basis or justification for it. And I did go back last night, and I literally mean last night, and pulled out the Chamber's order on the 27th of September, 2006, titled, "Order to admit Defence exhibit -- Defence evidence -" excuse me - "relevant to Christopher Beese," and in that ruling the Trial Chamber very specifically set out the law for this case, the rules to be followed in this case, the Prlic case, on tu quoque, and at page 3, for instance, the Chamber said, "The Chamber recalls established Tribunal jurisprudence where the principle of tu quoque does not apply to international humanitarian law and the obligations generated by this body of law have been designed to safeguard fundamental human values and therefore must be complied with regardless of the conduct of the other party or parties." The Chamber went on to say: "Considering that the documents related -- relating to the atrocities committed against the Croats of Bosnia would only be admitted if they intend to disprove any of the allegations made in the indictment; considering that unless the Defence shows to the Chamber how these documents tend to disprove any of the allegations made in the indictment and thus have a degree of relevance to the case, the Chamber will not admit it into the case; considering that for the remainder of the trial if the Defence moves for the admission through a witness," and I would submit this goes to also not just exhibits but to cross-examination or examination of a witness, "of a document relating to such -- to the atrocities committed against Croatian civilians in Bosnia, the Chamber shall request that the counsels for the Defence explain each time and before presenting such a document to the witness the reason for presenting it to the witness." That is, why is it relevant? Why are we going to spend precious court time on a question or an exhibit unless there is some showing of relevance to the issues in the case? And finally in the same 27 September 2006 order, the last full paragraph the Chamber in its ruling says: "Request that in future the counsels for the Defence explain in advance that the relevance for this case of questions put to a witness," let me repeat that, "in the case of questions put to a witness and the documents aimed at proving that atrocities were committed against the Croats in Bosnia," a basis for that. And, Your Honour, again crimes were committed by Muslims in Bosnia. Terrible things happened, and we can all condemn that. I condemn that. But the Chamber has ruled quite properly following Tribunal law as to tu quoque, and the Prosecution is concerned that we're spending an increasing amount of courtroom time on issues that are not relevant to the case, that are not defences to this case. And while I can understand that someone says the other side did it too so that's okay, that is not, that is not the law. And I would also before I go on to a separate topic, Your Honour, I would also say although it's not my function or job to assist is the Defence, of course, nor theirs to assist me, I'm not sure it's really helpful to establish in the courtroom that everyone was doing it, because if everyone was doing it, then I submit, I suggest that that makes it all the more likely that the HVO was doing it too, because "everyone was doing it." So that's my submission, Your Honour, on the tu quoque issue, and I would appreciate the Chamber's further guidance on that. Much more briefly, I need to turn to the Court's -- come back, as we mentioned yesterday, the Court's ruling on the exclusion of the witness -- excuse me, the evidence of this witness, Gerritsen, on the bridge, that there was some confusion about yesterday. I need, Your Honour, to understand further the Chamber's ruling or rationale for that. I have to, of course on an ongoing basis, decide how to present the Prosecution case and what procedures and tools are available to do that and whether it's viva voce evidence or 92 ter or whatever else the applicable rule or procedure may be, I have to direct the Prosecution team to make the best use of its time and the available tools, and it was not -- it is not clear to me from anything that was said yesterday, with all great respect, of what the nature of the ruling was. If -- was it because the witness was called as a 92 ter witness? I don't know. If that was the basis, Your Honour, then we need to know that, because then that suggests that the Prosecution cannot effectively use the 92 ter rule if there's going to be anything, any additional evidence outside the statement. Now, that may be the Chamber's ruling, but I'd like to be very clear that is the Chamber's ruling. If the Chamber's ruling was based on something else, I'm asking, I'm simply inviting the Chamber to give the Prosecution, and for that matter all the parties, additional guidance on to the basis of its ruling so that we can guide our conduct and future presentation accordingly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President; good afternoon, Your Honours. I would like to briefly respond to the Prosecution's allegations that the Defence is engaged in a everyone-did-it defence or a tu quoque defence specifically in relevance to or relation to the testimony elicited on cross-examination from the gentleman yesterday. I can -- I'll speak for myself. Others, if they want to pipe up, they can do so, but yesterday, the topics that were raised had to do with reverse ethnic cleansing. It had to do with the manipulation of media and how the international organisations were being manipulated, and of course that's relevant because we seem to be accepting wholesale documents from the international organisations, and I dare say that it's usually the case that if it comes from the UN, this being a UN institution, somehow it has a certain cachet value, and I dare say as the case is progressing and the more I'm involved in these sorts of cases I'm coming to recognise that anything coming out of the UN must be looked at with great scrutiny and not simply be accepted. Another issue that was raised was the -- the holding of hostages, in a sense, of the Muslim population, civilian population, by the Muslim army itself. That was important, as well as the so-called perception that the ABiH -- the Sarajevo government was actually for a -- a unified country and was the legitimate government when, in fact, what we see is they are inviting Croats to stay in certain areas in essence so they can hold them hostage or use them for -- in order to take humanitarian aid and sell it. The other issue was Uzdol. Now, Uzdol was important, in my opinion, because we heard a witness, we heard a witness that -- in rebuttal. The Prosecution wanted to explain to us that this gentleman could not possibly be one-sided, biased, or what have you, because after all he had been working for this organisation and had devoted his time to it. But he told us that, when he went to Uzdol, then what happened and how he was treated and how the Croats, and I underscore that because in my opinion that gentleman was biased against the Croats or Bosnia-Herzegovina, how they were uncaring, how they were unwilling to assist him because they wouldn't show him anything, and yet we see that this gentleman here went to Uzdol two days before, invited by the mayor, the same person who invited the other gentleman, invited a female journalist and was provided access to get all the information. Now, does that go to the credibility of the witness? Obviously. Everything that was raised by this particular Defence had nothing to do with tu quoque. It goes to credibility. Now, let me speak about credibility for one second. Yesterday there was an objection raised by Judge Trechsel regarding going beyond the scope of a direct examination. I understand the ruling, and the ruling is based on federal Rules of Evidence 611. Now, in that case, under rule 611, if you look at it, it will say also that you can go beyond the scope of direct examination if it goes to credibility. So areas that I was going into, on the one hand, I believed were within the scope, and if they were slightly outside the scope, we're dealing with issues of credibility. So if it's either this witness or other witnesses. Nonetheless, I took His Honour's objection to -- to my asking certain questions that appeared to be outside the scope. I didn't think it was, but nonetheless, I asked open-ended questions in conformity with the ruling. And as I noted to Judge Trechsel, sometimes you do have to ask a leading question at least to point the witness to what it is that you want to ask and then elicit questions by open-ended method. But Federal Rule of Evidence 611, which is what I understand this whole notion is based on, this new ruling, because at least that's what the -- when it first came up, it came up that there was a particular rule of evidence in the United States. It happens to be 611, so I raise that. But let me reiterate. There was nothing in the cross-examination that went to a everybody's-doing-it defence or to a tu quoque defence, and I don't think that my colleague in the Stojic Defence did that as well, and they can speak for themselves, but I didn't hear anything of that nature. With respect to the second issue that was raised by the Prosecution, I'm glad that they raised it. I've raised it before. I'll raise it again in a slightly different flavour. I'm concerned, I am concerned that the Trial Chamber has announced, having looked at the Prosecution's list, redacted list, revised list, I'm concerned that the Trial Chamber's announcement that they would perhaps be calling some of the Prosecution witnesses if the Prosecution didn't call them. Now, if the Trial Chamber does not give the Prosecution sufficient time to put on certain witnesses they believe are central to their case, then obviously they have to make certain choices. They do that with documents. They do that with their cross-examination -- their direct examination. They will do that with their witnesses. That's what any prudent lawyer would do whether they're on the Prosecution or on the Defence side. What I am concerned, however, is that the Trial Chamber has already predetermined that certain witnesses are essential and that if the Prosecution doesn't call them, then in essence what will happen is the Trial Chamber will be conducting a rebuttal of the Prosecution's case immediately after the taking of the evidence of the Defence, assuming there are defence cases. So I also think we need some guidance here, and I think that rather than take that approach, I think that the better approach would be perhaps to reconsider and have the Prosecution take another look, provided that the Judges are willing to -- to express and give confidence to the Prosecution how much additional time they may have beyond the redacted 107 hours that was decided earlier. So that was -- that's my response to the Prosecution's second issue. It's not quite on point, but it's related to the same thing, that both of us -- both sides need to have more confidence in how much time we will have, and I certainly am raising it now. I will be raising it again. But I find it troublesome that the Trial Chamber is already -- has already made a determination that it needs to hear Prosecution witnesses and in essence the -- while it is not giving time to the Prosecution to put on its case it will be acting as if it were a Prosecutor in conducting a rebuttal. That's the impression that we get on this side. I know it's -- may not be the intention, but that's what -- that's the impression that we have on this side. And I don't think that's -- that would be appropriate. It's one thing if the Prosecution were to decide not to call a particular witness because they chose not to do so, but when they're unable to call witnesses because they're not provided the time by the Trial Chamber, then I think we're robbing Peter to pay Paul. We're taking time from them, but then we're going to give their time to the Prosecution after the Defence case, and after the Defence has precluded them. And if we look at the Rules of this Tribunal with respect to rebuttal evidence, which is a correct approach, it deviates from the approach that we take in the United States, for instance, where the Prosecution can withhold vital information, can -- or vital witnesses or evidence and use it on rebuttal. Here, rebuttal is strictly rebuttal. It is not to bolster a case. So -- and I think that calling witnesses afterwards by the Trial Chamber would be for the purposes of bolstering the Prosecution case. And while the Prosecution stood up and indicated that they felt that at least the Bench or one member of the Bench maybe leaning one way or the other, we think, at least I think, the Prlic Defence team thinks that this approach would give a clear signal that perhaps it is unintended by the ruling. So therefore, I would suggest that -- that if you feel that there is a need for certain witnesses, to give the time to the Prosecution to call those witnesses. Let them call. So then we can decide what case we're going to put on to rebut that case it puts us in a better position. We're not saying we shouldn't hear from them, but let's hear from them as part of the Prosecution case. So then we can determine how we're going to structure our own cases. And also, it goes to the period of time that we will need to decide how many witnesses we will be putting on, if any. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I shall not answer all you've said, Mr. Karnavas, but I must to set straight a misunderstanding which apparently already occurred yesterday. I refer you to line 100 -- to page 100, line 19 of yesterday's transcript, and I quote myself. I said: "I'm not saying you can't ask him what you're asking him." I did not object to the substance of the questions. I just objected to the form. And there I did not refer to any foreign, including American, law, but I refer to paragraph 13 of a decision taken by this Chamber on the 10th of May of this year. I wanted to set this straight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I totally understood. And I wasn't saying that you were preventing me from going into an area. With respect to federal rule 611, it is my understanding from previous occasions, what I've heard from the Trial Bench, that the recent ruling is in part based on that rule of evidence, which -- obviously the Trial Chamber is free to look at various foreign jurisdictions. So that was my -- and then I just wanted to give some guidance as far as my understanding, and that's why I felt that even if it's -- if I'm asking questions that go beyond the scope but deal with credibility, the form of the question can still be leading under federal rule 611. And my -- and what I believed I was doing was going into areas of credibility. But at the end of the day, I take the point. I understand the ruling, and feel free to correct me if you think I've strayed and have gone off the reservation, pull me back in. I don't have a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just a very small point. I would not say "based on," but inspired by Rule 6 [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. There you go. I think we understand each other totally. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. First of all, in response to Mr. Scott's point about tu quoque, I think he misses an important distinction. The -- the Prosecution, I think, would like the Trial Chamber to look at this case in a vacuum or in a -- in a very black and white way, to say that we can focus only on acts which were committed, or apparently committed, by members of the HVO and to ignore the context in which the conflict was taking place, and that's really a very -- with all respect to my good friend, Mr. Scott, a very naive way to look at the case, because this is a very complex situation. The Prosecution's allegations are not confined to a series of individual crimes committed by one side or the other; in this case, the Bosnian Croats. The Prosecution's allegation is that there was a wide-ranging joint criminal enterprise which, if I understand it, involves nothing less than effectively the annexation by the Bosnian Croats or the attempted annexation of a significant portion of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina with the ultimate aim of ethnically cleansing that territory and perhaps even causing it to be joined in some manner with Republic of Croatia in due course. That's -- that's the scope of this case. And against that, we must be free to invite the Trial Chamber to look at what the HVO was facing, what the government, as it were, of Herceg-Bosna was facing, what the military situation was, what the political situation was. And just to focus on one or two examples, that -- not to repeat what Mr. Karnavas said, but when you're looking at an allegation of reverse ethnic cleansing or an alleged plan to -- to -- for the Bosnian Croats to remove their own population from A to B in pursuance of redesigning the ethnicity of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the Trial Chamber is then suddenly confronted with the fact of military activity on the part of the ABiH which completely explains the movement of population, but incidentally involves the commission of what may be crimes by individual members of the armija. That's something that we have to look at. It's not to do with tu quoque. Nobody's saying, at least Stojic Defence is certainly not saying that if one side did it, it's all right for the other side to do it. What we're saying is that you have to look at this situation holistically. You have to put yourself in the position of those accused and say, what was the situation they were facing here? Because this case is not about individual perpetrators. We're not -- we're not doing the Tuta and Stela case here. We're doing -- none of these men went out and personally committed crimes. The issue here is one of political and military leaders, and you have to understand the whole situation. Now, there may be individual circumstances where the Trial Chamber says well, perhaps we didn't need to go into that. Perhaps that was something that we really didn't need to hear. And we're doing our best to make our case relevant in terms of what we present, as does the Prosecution. Both sides from time to time may stray from the path of what is strictly relevant and we hope that the Trial Chamber will bring that to our attention, but we do try to present you with a case that is relevant and presents the whole picture. A good example yesterday when my colleague, Ms. Nozica, was cross-examining and she crew the witnesses attention to a Prosecution exhibit 9629. It drew an objection. Why are we going into Bugojno? Why are we looking at this? And as Ms. Nozica pointed out, events were going on in Bugojno at the same time they were going on in Prozor. These were not isolated events taking place on two different continents. They were going on a very short distance apart and they were interconnected, and that's what Ms. Nozica was trying to -- to bring out. I don't have any response. I'm sure Mr. Kovacic will want to address the issue of bridges so I won't get into that. I -- Somehow we got into the question of rebuttal and the Prosecution calling witnesses, or the Trial Chamber. I'm not sure how we got into that, but we since we have got into it, let me just make one point, which is that the position that I will be asking the Trial Chamber to take in due course is this: Under Rule 98 bis, when this comes time for motions for judgements of acquittal, that Rule stipulates that these motions shall be heard and determined at the close of the Prosecutor's case, and it will be the submission of the Stojic Defence that that means when the Prosecution closes its case and not when additional witnesses may be called by the Trial Chamber. We submit that it's the obligation of the Prosecution to present their case fully within the time allotted because this is an adversarial proceeding. Your Honour, I don't want to take any more time. If there are specific questions, of course, I would be glad to answer them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wish to say that I support everything my colleagues have said, so I will be very brief. I especially wish to support the points made by Mr. Murphy. I do allow that it may appear sometimes to the Prosecutor that the Defence is using tu quoque, but this is not the case, quite evidently. I think it is quite clear to Your Honours that these six Defence teams, at least the Defence team of General Praljak, fully agree with what my colleague has said and what Your Honours wrote in the decision you handed down. Tu quoque cannot be an acceptable defence, and there is no need to discuss that. My colleague, Mr. Murphy, gave two or three examples. Since superficially our defence case may appear to be tu quoque unless one goes into the whole history of this case. I especially support something my colleague has said which I myself was going to say. These proceedings relating to the events mentioned in the indictment refer to events which happened not in a vacuum but in a certain context. The conclusions that Your Honours will one day have to reach about legally relevant facts should be drawn from the context of certain events. If we wish to reach realistic conclusions, we cannot view the context in the way that is often applied in this Tribunal. In one case there's an accused belonging to one of the armies participating in the conflict. In another case there is another. We cannot avoid pointing to the actual situation as it was on the ground. I will add something else to what my colleague has said. Bearing in mind that a joint criminal enterprise is alleged to have existed, it is alleged that there was a certain plan and certain conclusions are drawn from this. Some actions are seen as stemming from that plan, and our defence wishes to demonstrate that there was no such plan, no such enterprise. So when we are pointing to the broader context of events, this is to show that the decisions made by certain people within the HZ HB or the HV or O were a consequence of certain events. They were responses to certain events that took place. Once side did one thing. Another side is trying to solve the problem that arose for them. That is not tu quoque. It's real life, and we are trying to draw from real life the relevant conclusions concerning the culpability of the accused. But when we know what the events are, then we can judge about the mens rea. Another example which I think is perhaps quite self-evident is a situation in which there was a murder or looting in a village. For example, burning, looting, murders in a village. All the events in that village take place in a certain time, in a certain context. If there was fighting in that village we have to first show that there was another armed side there; secondly, that there was a war on, and then, only then, can we conclude whether a civilian who might have been killed was collateral damage or whether there was a plan to kill those civilians. So is it tu quoque if the Defence is trying to prove that there was a certain military unit in a certain village, that there was fighting going on or, for instance, that the areas of Jablanica and Mostar were interlinked as regards the war events? Because if we don't know that, we will not be able to reach conclusions about the relevant facts. Another reason why we sometimes enter into these matters which are erroneously seen as tu quoque is also the credibility of certain witnesses, to check how familiar the witnesses were with the situation, to check how objective the witnesses were, how impartial they were, since we have had witnesses here who simply did not see certain events, but they saw others that the Prosecutor is interested in. I won't go further into that area. Furthermore, as regards my learned friend's objection, I think that the issue of the bridge which was later introduced into the statement of the witness, I think that question is closed with Your Honour's ruling of yesterday. I only wish to tell Your Honours that we have eliminated from our planned cross-examination anything that refers to that point because we feel in view of Your Honour's ruling that this is justified and that we need not go into it further with this witness. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you for giving me leave to speak. I will not repeat what my colleagues have said, especially Mr. Murphy. I fully agree with what they have said. I only wish to say the following: If, on behalf of the OTP, my learned friend, Mr. Scott, is saying that there is no doubt that members of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina committed crimes, it would be very important for us in our case if Mr. Scott were to confirm that he does not deny that among the Croatian population on the territory which came under the control of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina due to the offensive actions of that army, there was justified fear and that those who left those areas left because of this justified fear. In that case, the Defence will have no questions about the events in Bugojno or any other place which came under the control of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Until the Prosecutor states this, we feel duty-bound to prove that Croats did not leave for no reason, of their own free will, but that they left out of fear and that their fear was justified, that their departure was for a justified reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't wish to add anything. I just wish to say on behalf of the Coric Defence that we agree with everything said so far and that we also join in what has been said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. One minute. I'm not going to belabour any of the things as said. I know everyone's anxious to get on with the evidence but two very quick responses. I understand -- I mean, to be intellectually honest and fair, I understand the issue of context. Let me just say, there is context and then there is context, and everyone knows that it can become so large and so broad as the exception swallows the rule or to say, at least a saying in the English language, and I'm sure there must be equivalents in French and German and Hungarian and all the other languages in the courtroom, the exception becomes so large that you could drive a truck through it. That's what we say where I came -- or at least where come from. And, yes, there is context, but there have to be limitations on -- on that concept somewhere, number one. Number two, I'm afraid that the question about the bridge may have somewhat become more lost in some of the broader points and discussions that were being made, including by Mr. Karnavas, on some other topics that indeed are important topics but not the ones that the Prosecution raised this afternoon. I'm not trying to -- please do not think that I'm trying to reargue at this point the Chamber's ruling. I'm simply asking to know about the nature of the ruling itself so that we can guide our conduct in the future. Let me make it very specific. If the Chamber's ruling were to be that the Prosecution was not allowed to ask questions about the bridge because it was outside the statement and because the witness was caused -- called as a 92 ter witness, that will affect the way that we call witnesses in the future, because what the Chamber has said, with the greatest respect, is if the Prosecution had called this witness as a viva voce witness, that evidence would have been allowed. Therefore, we should have called him as a viva voce witness, but in the other -- but if there is some other ruling, Your Honour, then we would invite the Chamber to at least grant both us and the parties more guidance on this point, because we have to call other witnesses in the future, and again, Your Honour, we think that the mixed -- what the Prosecution has called a mixed use of the Rule is a process that makes sense, that's been followed in other cases where certain evidence of a witness is tendered in writing by the statement under 92 ter, and there maybe certain additional or different evidence by the same witness that is presented viva voce. That seems to us like a straightforward concept, but I fear that perhaps we seem not to come to agreement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. First, let's talk about the bridge. I am under the impression that it's a storm in a teacup. The problem was the following: The witness was called to be questioned regarding a statement that he had given to the Prosecutor on the 25th of April and on the 7th of May, 2002. That statement is a summary under Rule 65 ter was disclosed to the Defence. In that statement, at no time the witness talks about the destruction of the Old Bridge. So he did not talk about it. So the general rule is that when a witness is called here, he is questioned on his written statement and not on other elements that do not -- that are not comprised in the written statement. So that was the first point. The Chamber noticed, furthermore, that that witness, on the 9th of November, was not in Mostar. Therefore, why put questions to him about the Old Bridge, whereas that person was not present while the Old Bridge -- when the Old Bridge was destroyed? So for legal reasons and for practical reasons, we deemed that it was not adequate to put questions to that witness on those points, notwithstanding 92 ter, the 92 ter procedure. I also thought that, aside from 92 ter and that procedure, you wanted to introduce the additional element the Old Bridge, and this is why the Defence opposed to this new introduction. The Chamber limited the questioning, whether it be viva voce or 92 ter, to the written statement. You are worried about the future. There is no problem for the future. In the future, if there is some points that you would like to raise, you may raise those points according to the statement of the witnesses, but we don't have to call a witness to put question to the witness on a topic that was not raised during the proofing session and during -- and in his written statement. So that was that first point. So please rest assured that there are no problems here, and you do not have to worry for the future. It is obviously clear that if this witness had come or seemed to be a very important witness because he was, let's say, an eyewitness to the destruction of the Old Bridge, the Judges would have asked him the questions. As it already happened when you have witnesses who are called to the bar, we can deem it necessary to ask a question, to put a question to the witness, but it was not the case in this particular case. So please rest assured there are absolutely no problems with regard to the decision that we've rendered. The second point, the second issue, the issue of the tu quoque. In fact what you said is -- makes perfect sense, but what Mr. Murphy said is also important. There are some events that took place in time, and some events can only be understood if one understands what happened before. As an example, if, for instance, does an influx of refugees in Prozor, why was there an influx of refugees? Maybe this happened because in Bugojno there was a BiH offensive which made it so that the population was moving. So in order to understand this particular example, you have to go understand why the -- why this happened. Sometimes the Defence may waste time, and this can be very quickly explained to the Chamber by putting one or two questions to the witness, but I also noticed that sometimes we waste time in order to try to explain an event that would be very easy to explain by putting one or two questions rather than spending hours on trying to explain things by putting all sorts of questions that are not targeted questions. So it is very easy to put a targeted question and say whatever happened in village A was a consequence of what happened in village B. So -- and let me go back to what Mr. Karnavas said. I was mostly struck by what -- this particular topic, the question of the witnesses who are called by the Court. Mr. Karnavas said that the Chamber is bringing Prosecution witnesses. That is not our opinion. The Chamber would call witnesses who would come here because of the interest of justice, to understand what happened. Similarly, when the Defence will present the list of their witnesses, if it seems that on that list there are important witnesses that the Defence does not wish to call or removes at the last minute, we will say why. Why? Well, because this witness seems to be important to us. Do not forget that the Trial Chamber has the responsibility to render a judgement. This judgement has to be motivated. The Chamber does not have the right to commit mistakes. And in order to avoid to commit mistakes on facts, the Chamber must have in its possession all the elements, and this is why the Rule stipulated that Judges may call, provides for the Judges to call witnesses and can also ask witnesses to bring additional elements. So we have that mission. If we do not hold on to this mission, it will be something that can be considered as a miscarriage of justice. So if we start -- if we think that way, we can notice that the Prosecution made a list of witnesses under Rule 65 ter. We can also notice that some witnesses are not planned or not on the list. Some witnesses were removed from the list. There can be also time constraint issues which does not allow us to bring forward all the witnesses, to call all the witnesses to the bar. But as I already explained in my individual opinion, it is up to the Prosecution to choose carefully its witnesses. When there's a witness, A, B, and C in an X entity, it is better to call Witness A who was in charge of the entity rather than have Witness C that was number three in this organisation. And rather than calling A, B, and C together, maybe Witness A would be sufficient. So in fact, one has to make a choice, a very judicial choice that would allow the Chamber to have a global image on what happened and eventually on the irresponsibilities. And we are as Mr. Murphy indicated so well, we are dealing with a case where we military responsibilities and political. When we talk about the military responsibilities, there is a hierarchy and it goes there the top of the military command and it goes all the way down to the last soldier on the field. In that hierarchy, each person plays a role, and a professional Judge must ask himself the question when an event takes place, what were the mechanisms that existed in what hierarchy? And if we realise there are some holes, one can be surprised, astonished at a certain soldier that belonged to the hierarchy is not there to bring his testimony. And as an example, once again I would like to cite the case of Stupni Do. Something happened. There was a hierarchy in place. There's a chain of command. A person was -- the person pled guilty. The person was accused, and it would be good that that person be here so they could explain what happened, because that person was part of a chain of command. Did that person act under an order? Did that person act individually? What happened? A Trial Chamber composed of professional Judges has these responsibilities and cannot judge, for instance, the Stupni Do case without at least hearing witnesses who are appropriate witnesses. So the question that we have to ask ourselves is the following: At what point when the Chamber notices that witnesses are missing, when can the Chamber call these witnesses? The articles in the Rules is not very clear. Those witnesses, to me, can come at any point, even before the 98 bis phase, but they can also be called to the bar at the very end. There are different practices. For instance, in the Blaskic case the witnesses came at the very end. In the Hadzihasanovic and Kubura case, we have heard witnesses before the 98 bis procedure. I'm not going to quote other cases, but this is just to give you an example. And contrary could what Mr. Karnavas says, what the Trial Chamber calls a witness, the Trial Chamber does not think that this is a Prosecution witness. It is a witness, period. And that type of witness can also be beneficial for the Defence, for instance. So when the Chamber decides to call a witness, it is to show the truth, and it is not so that one or the other party can benefit from the presence of that witness. So I really hope that Mr. Karnavas understood what the -- what is the procedure that the Judges of these -- this Tribunal adopt. When they call a witness to the bar is to have an absolute clarity of what happened but not to favour one party or the other or not to place one party in a bad light. This is what I wanted to say with regard to 98 bis, Rule 98 bis. This is why Judges can call witnesses. In order to summarise, you have expressed your points of view. There is no discrepancies, in fact, on what you said. I thank Mr. Murphy for what he told us. He was very clear and always, as usual, very knowledgeable in terms of legal and -- legal matters. And Mr. Scott who intervened in tu quoque issue, I think that what he wanted to say is to notice that a lot of time was dedicated to this issue. The Defence also explained in what light they were using that particular strategy, and I must say that at times I have also noticed that much time has been taken to deal with questions that would have been really easy to demonstrate without too much relying on documents, and especially by the fact that many questions are asked or put to various witnesses. If we have one credible witness who answered correctly and who is a credible witness, it is not necessary to put the same questions to another witness who say the same thing. But that, of course, is up to the Defence. They have the choice. They can choose the strategy they wish, and it's up to them to decide what they wish to do. Mr. Stewart was on his feet at one point but he did not intervene. I'm going to hand him the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's kind of you, Your Honour; thank you. Now, I did, of course, want to hear what Your Honour said first, naturally. Your Honour, it's a very brief observation; it's this: That a decision - I'm not entering into the details of submissions and so on, on Chamber witnesses - but any decision to call a Chamber witness in exercise of the duties of the Trial Chamber is potentially quite a significant decision, and my plea, Your Honour, and what I particularly urge is that before any such decisions are taken that Your Honours do indicate plenty of time in advance and do give the parties the full opportunity of making submissions. Your Honour, it is, and I register a mild protest here, it has been a protest by others and by me on behalf of Mr. Petkovic, that sometimes decisions are taken without an adequate opportunity. And may I just comment that the decision that came up earlier against leading questions in cross-examination where the cross-examination goes outside the scope of examination-in-chief was a decision made after I had specifically said on an occasion that it was a matter which, in my submission, required more consideration and more submission, and, Your Honour, it's only fair to the parties if we don't take time under time pressures on a particular occasion but we do register that before a decision is taken we would wish to make full submissions. It's only fair that we are then given that opportunity before those decisions are taken. I'm not saying -- who knows what the decision would have been, but the deprivation of the opportunity to make submissions on questions before they are decided is simply not fair. So, Your Honour, that's a general observation. I do urge the Trial Chamber not to fall into that practice, but in relation to Chamber witnesses, it is terribly important. In some cases -- I will just comment. In some cases the procedure adopted has ended up verging on the ludicrous or the farcical, but that's a submission to be developed, no doubt, another day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Stewart, please rest assured, regarding the witnesses of the Chamber, no decision was taken yet, and we did not even discuss it amongst us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's understood, Your Honour. My comment was for future reference, and I rather feel it's been noted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No translation, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have stated -- do we have interpretation? Yes, we do. Yes. I stated that with regard to the witnesses, no decision has been taken yet, and we have not even considered the matter amongst ourselves. But you're worried about the future. Well, as for the future, we've asked the Prosecution, following the decision rendered by the Appeals Chamber, to provide us with the schedule for the Prosecution witnesses for the time left. The Prosecution will provide us with a schedule with the names of the witnesses, X, Y, Z. Then we'll consider whether some other witnesses might be necessary, and of course we'll tell you about it and you'll have the opportunity to make submissions then. But for the time being it's not possible, because the Prosecution has not provided us with that schedule yet. We are just considering the matter at this stage, and we are eagerly expecting the schedule that the Prosecution has promised that they will provide us. But I believe my colleague wants to talk as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, a small point has not been answered that was raised by you, Mr. Scott. You wondered whether the issue of the bridge destruction had been denied because the witness was presented as a 92 ter witness. I can clearly tell you that this is not the case. The only consideration of the Chamber was in fact that this was a proposal taking the Defence by surprise hours or less before the witness would appear. The Chamber also took into account that the time for this witness had been reduced, in view of the arrival of another witness tomorrow. These are the reasons, but not the fact that the witness was presented under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me just say that I appreciate, Mr. President, both you and the Chamber and Judge Trechsel's comments on that, and that I do thank the Chamber for being responsive to -- to the inquiry. Whether we agreed with it or not, it helps the parties to understand and plan their witnesses accordingly. So I do thank the Chamber for that additional guidance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It would probably be very useful to have a break now so that we can start the cross-examination after the break. It is already 3.20. So let's take a 20-minute break, and we will resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The hearing is resumed. Colonel, we apologise for this delay. We had a procedural question to debate. Before your arrival, before you start your testimony today, we had to resolve some issues, and this is why you're here -- we are late. I will now like to hand the floor to the Defence. I don't know who is going to start. Is it Ms. Alaburic, or is it Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. By your leave, I would like to begin my cross-examination, but I will leave most of this time to General Praljak. I think I need not go into the reasons in great detail. I believe this is in accordance with Your Honours' decision, and that his examination will fall within the scope of the leave granted by Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Witness. I am the Defence counsel for General Praljak. I will put a few questions to you, and then, with Their Honours' leave, General Praljak will put some questions to you directly. Yesterday, an issue was raised linked to the chief of the ECMM in the regional centre of Zenica, an ambassador whose name I will not mention here. I will just put one question in this regard. Could we please have in e-court 3D 00330. Witness, you have a binder before you. This document should be at the top. It's not part of the binder. It should be on top of the pile. Yes, that's the document. This is an excerpt from a book written by the military historian Charles Shrader, whom we consider to be expert. He has written a book about the war in Central Bosnia, and I shall draw your attention to page 0262, or in the original book page 55. This is the paragraph above the subtitle "Communications." Towards the end of this paragraph I will read the quotation in connection with which I want to put some questions to you. I quote: "[In English] [Previous translation continues] ... for reasons that are not entirely clear that the ECMM monitors in Central Bosnia generally favoured the Muslims, even to the extent of minimising Croat charges of ethnic cleansing by the Muslims and accusing the HVO of using women and children to rob UN aid convoys." Before I put my question, I would like to look at the footnote marked here, footnote 73. You have it on the next page. There's no need to read the entire footnote. The author refers to the document on the basis of which he makes this assertion, and he says the following: "[In English] By my measurements, Ambassador Thebault was thoroughly anti-Croat in word and deed, but his successor, Britain's Sir Martin Garrod, was much more evenhanded." [Interpretation] Witness, Mr. Gerritsen, in connection with the first part of this assessment, this author feels that the ECMM was in a way not objective with respect to the Croats and that, as a consequence, there was mutual mistrust. The HVO did not have much confidence in the ECMM and vice versa. The ECMM was quick to blame the HVO whenever an incident occurred. Can you confirm that during the time you were there you felt, at least on occasion, the distrust of the HVO in relation to the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- first I must say my personal feelings about this. I always try to be independent, and that's also the formal point of view of the ECMM. In the circumstances at that time, it's difficult to operate, and on both sides there were -- there was a lot of mistrust against ECMM but also against UNPROFOR. I have a case with the mayor of Prozor, Mr. Jozic, which he didn't trust UNPROFOR, and that was the reason I was invited, firstly, and personally, for the massacre in Uzdol, which was -- was not liked by Graham Binns, the company commander of the Prince of Wales Own Regiment of Yorkshire located in Gornji Vakuf. But after some communication between ECMM, UNPROFOR, and Mr. Jozic, he was also allowed to join the 15th of September. This is an example for the opposite. I do understand. Regarding Mr. Thebault --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gerritsen, perhaps I will put a specific question to you regarding Mr. Thebault, just to expedite matters and to go step-by-step. In the view of this author, the author of this book, Ambassador Thebault, if I might paraphrase the author of the book, was simply not objective. You were one the monitors preparing reports on various events. We've heard about all this. And inter alia, you sent these reports to the regional centre. Some were directly forwarded to Zagreb, but some reports sent by you and your team from Gornji Vakuf were integrated into more comprehensive reports, either by topic or by time. Would it be true to say that you did not always agree with Ambassador Thebault's assessments and, if so, what was the source of the disagreement? What was the disagreement about?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that I wasn't always very pleased with the assessments because they were fairly short, but I have no examples now. So I can only tell the feeling I had at that time, the feelings, and that's more on an abstract level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My feeling at that time was that UNPROFOR, and also Mr. Hauenstein, my colleague, and ECMM in Zenica represented by Mr. Thebault, were maybe not deliberately but more in favour with the Muslims, as was the international community at that time then in favour with the Croats. It was a point that wasn't be discussed, that couldn't be discussed, because no one would say so. So we have to look into the files and make our conclusion -- conclusions from that side. I can only say my point of view. I did it before in this statement that I try to be independent, and in that way even when we made our daily reports in the evening we had a lot of discussions what would be put into the report. I had the discussions with Peter Hauenstein. But I can't recall now specific things. That's -- that's the difficulty. Then I should see all the daily reports from my own, and I have them, but also look into the daily reports from Travnik and Zenica, because I haven't studied these matters from this particular point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. I think your answer is clear. It is precisely the point I was trying to make. I will not delve further into this matter. I simply wanted to confirm the standpoint of the author of this book in order to introduce a realistic note. Let's now have document 3D 00991. Mr. Gerritsen, Colonel Gerritsen, you have the document in your binder. 00991.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's Croat or Bosnian? Yes, I have 3D 00991, but it's not in the English language. Can someone help me out?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [In English] It is first on Croatian language, and then it is English.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, it's opposite. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any case, you don't have it in the original because I assume you wrote it in Dutch. However, we had it translated into English and B/C/S. Witness, let me first put a question to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, on this document we see the address and the phone number of the witness. You should have made sure not to show them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just about to ask the witness, Your Honour. In view of the fact that this was sent for publication, I was about to ask the witness whether he wished the document to be under seal, but the witness's address should certainly be redacted. However, maybe if it was published it need not all be in private session. I, however, wish to ask the witness, by your leave, Your Honours. So could not broadcast the front page, registrar, please, and then we'll see with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Gerritsen, first of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. A very small technical question. Would you happen to have a copy of the original in the Dutch language?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately not, Your Honour. We received the document from the OTP in English and in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Colonel, first let me ask you, regardless of the fact that the article seems to have been published, if you wish, Witness, we can have this in private session, although I see no reason why it should not be broadcast, but I leave it up to you, Witness. I will only ask you questions about the second paragraph under the subtitle, "Which Atrocities."

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will not ask to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I draw your attention to page 1 of your letter. Not the cover page, which is a fax, but page 1. There is a subtitle here, "Which Atrocities," and there are two paragraphs below it, and the second paragraph begins with, "[In English] People change under the influence of violence. I have been able to observe this clearly in others. Soldiers were changed over approximately 2 weeks ..." [Interpretation] So on and so forth. Could you please read it to yourself, this whole paragraph. Well, we can leave out the last two sentences, and then I will put a question to you. If you have read this.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This is a description you gave of what you saw and felt regarding the behaviour of soldiers and officers in the field. Can you tell Their Honours whether you stand by what you wrote then today?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's still the same for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And my last question in this respect: Do you agree that in the circumstances of this kind of war, and your observations are excellent and very interesting, is it easy or even possible with such men -- seen from the viewpoint of officers, is it easy to command and control such men, enforce law and order as would be normal under more normal circumstances? Would you agree that the officers and men participating in this conflict in circumstances you were able to see for yourself were facing an impossible task, that it was actually impossible to enforce complete and full discipline? You are a soldier, so perhaps you can tell us something about this?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It needs very good skills for a leader to lead these kind of units who are in war. It's a matter of a lot of things. You should give a good example, of course, and all we have learned to do. But in a real war, it's always a mess. And the war is also deteriorating. That is a law of war. And it's hard to -- in each war to have disciplined men. Each country has problems with that. There are several examples of that, in America, in Vietnam, nowadays in Iraq, even also -- not even, also our army has problems with that -- had problems with that in Iraq, with the marines specifically. And I know that in our country we pay a lot of attention -- a lot of attention to these kind of problems. And when you send people to war, it's not possible to guide all men in a way that they would behave all as it should be pointed -- as it is pointed out in the book, according to the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And to round off this topic, one specific question more. You said that all armies have problems to a greater or lesser extent. Would you agree, and this seems to follow from what you've said, that only the best organised soldiers -- armies, the armies that have the longest tradition, the best training, are successful in fully controlling their men and enforcing discipline, whereas conversely, armies which are just being created cannot succeed in this in spite of the best will of their commanders? Would you agree with this proposition?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, one question on the document. You explained that you were taken hostage. You are talking about what event exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken hostage for just a couple of hours. I was at the end late in the evening sent home by the Muslims in Bugojno because of the fact I had a package from Mr. Siljeg in my car, and he asked me to bring it to an address, and I forgot this package and people who looked into the car from the ABiH saw the name of Mr. Siljeg above. And I drove further on, and then they took me -- the people of the ABiH army imprisoned me, pointed with their guns, with their weapons, and I think it were five people, five soldiers, and they brought me to the HQ from the ABiH in Bugojno where I stayed a couple of hours in a room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Your Honours, my client will now put questions, by your leave.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Colonel. After a long time we meet again, here. You are a soldier, so we will, I hope, go very quickly through some matters that might be of interest. Please look at 3D 00981. This document is an interim report sent by Colonel Siljeg to the commander of the main HVO staff, namely myself; I was in that position at that time. As you were referring to the situation in the army, this report, in my view, illustrates very well what this is all about. Please look at paragraph 2, point 2. "Instead of shortening the combat line in a planned manner by conquering individual elevations, we are dealing with internal problems, mainly raising the manpower levels up to the required level because of problems with the arrival of men from Ljubuski, Livno, and the latest problems relate to people from Jajce and the Lasva battalion. The people from Jajce are asking to be replaced if possible -- they want to rest in Tomislavgrad after their losses, and they want to be replaced by men from Klis and Kostajnica which are in Herzegovina. They -- the people from Lasva were reluctant to go to the positions in Kucani. The morale in these two units is at zero level. I don't know what to do. These people are -- the line is weak. They don't feel that this is their own territory. I don't know how long we can go on pushing them like this." We will skip over point 3. "There's no time to connect all this in the best manner. If we solve one problem another arises immediately," and so on and so forth. Let's look at point 4. It says, "The representatives of the European Community have put the following problems to me today. A, the military police in Rama won't let them see the hodza in Prozor. B, they want to visit the hospital in Uskoplje. C, they want to visit the prisoners of war in Prozor." Look at D. "Josip Kovacevic went to the Adriatic coast and abducted a Muslim family. He is holding them in Prozor to exchange them for his father who is imprisoned in Bugojno. The European Community considers him to be a terrorist. What to do?" And then there's mention of Vares and so on. He then says he needs help. There are fewer and fewer men. And because of individual soldiers leaving, especially men from Jajce, Sebesici, and Bugojno, who are difficult to control in all these problems as individuals. They simply leave the unit and they are not there on their shift. This is threatening the morale of the men on the front line. Last night we managed to bring back 10 to 15 men from Ljubuski, and we got them to hold on until today. There was nothing else we could do because half the company stayed at the positions for longer than four days, whereas all the others left five days ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, the witness had left one week ago, and I wonder how you will link this to the witness and what is the foundation for the -- you read an interesting letter. It's certainly interesting, but what could the witness contribute who had left one week before?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: If I may also add, what we have seen is General Praljak read through the letter but there is no question. I mean, we don't know why this document is being put to this witness. We all can read the contents of this lengthy document, but I don't believe that this is the correct way to approach the introduction of the document. I think that it should be done in such a way that the General should ask some introductory questions to ascertain whether or not the witness knows something about the contents of the document, and then he can ask him whether or not the document bears out what he has said. But merely to read the document in the manner in which he has done so, I don't think that's appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Praljak, please put your question to the witness. We've all -- we all have the document in front of us. All of us, including the witness, because you're wasting your own time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's very simple. Well, I can just keep quiet and have the witness read the document. But Judge Trechsel, in the army, seven days changes nothing. The fact that on the 22nd or 15th or whatever the date was, nothing much changes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, sir, Witness, Colonel, in your opinion to the best of your knowledge, was this how it was while you were up there? Did you have the same kind of problems as described by Colonel Siljeg? Could you see this on the ground as concerns the HVO forces and units?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and specifically the points in point 4. I know them and I was there. They are familiar for me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now the next document, 3D 00979, please. You have the document. You can read it. It's my response to the issues raised in paragraph 4 or point 4, sent to Mr. Siljeg on the 23rd of September. It says as follows under B: "Release them. And as far as the terrorist is concerned, inform the SIS and the military police." And the third was to change one of the commanders, replace one of the commanders. Can you tell me this: Within the frameworks of what one can control, did I - to the European Community, UNPROFOR and so on - always enable them to go to any location where you wanted to go? If I was present up there, of course. Did I always give permission for you to go where you wanted?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we could talk to Siljeg or to General Praljak, we get allowance, but it wasn't always possible to talk to them because they were in the terrain, or in the field, I mean. Is that the same, the terrain or field?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. So do you agree then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, in the document shown to you by General Praljak, there is a mention of the commander of a Kvaternik Brigade, Ivica Pavic. The -- General Praljak has not read out the sentence, but it is stated that Colonel Siljeg is not pleased, is not satisfied with his work because he's late. He's not accurate, and apparently he's drafting reports that are not accurate. Did you know that person? This Pavic person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In which point? 4? Pavic, no. I'm not aware of Pavic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: May I have 3D 00615 next, please. It's the document that you were shown yesterday by Counsel Nozica about the child, Haris Silajdzic, four and a half years old. We cleared that point up. We know that he was taken off. Now look at the second page of that document, because the document is a two-page document, in fact. It is 0023 -- 002. It is a certificate or confirmation from Split, and this is what the document says, that a medical commission met in Split and made their recommendations which were to continue treatment abroad, and the family was that of Haris Silajdzic, and it says that all these persons had no personal documents. And as they had to continue their treatment abroad, they needed a passport. And then they are requesting that a -- that passports shall issued so that the people can be treated abroad. And it is signed by Dr. Goran Dodig and the head nurse as well. Now, do you see the name Haris Silajdzic under number 3? Does it say Haris Silajdzic?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when I see it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Colonel, when we received the family, took the family in, did anybody give them any material resources, any money to play for the hospital in Split? The Bugojno municipality, for example, or the European monitors, perhaps, or the Red Cross. Did anybody give them anything except for the bundles that they received?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I know of. I didn't give them money.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, from this document it would appear that they have to continue their treatment abroad, which entails Croatian citizenship for them to be able to be issued passports and that those costs will be met by the Croatian state. Is something that -- is that something that you can see on the basis of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry for interrupting again General Praljak, but I fail to see how this has any relevance to the subject of the indictment. It's not disputed -- it's not disputed in any way that the Croat authorities assisted this leukaemia child and transported -- arranged for the transport, but this is not the subject of any dispute whatsoever, and I don't see any need to go into it in any further detail. It doesn't add anything to the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your purpose, Mr. Praljak? What do you want to prove? Do you want to prove that these Muslims had been treated in Croatia and that therefore they needed a passport where their nationality was indicated? But in the document you will see that members of the ABiH and the HVO, five of them, have also been treated. So I suppose that the members of the ABiH were not Croatian nationals. What do you want to establish, because it's very confusing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I want to prove is very simple, Your Honours. The system of hospitals, and I'll show you another document that will clear this matter up, is a system and organisation controlled by Dr. Franjo Tudjman and the Croatian government, and the passage through Herceg-Bosna is controlled by Slobodan Praljak, Bruno Stojic, Milivoj Petkovic, et cetera. These are all system that we control, and they said we are going to issue passports to everyone and pay for treatment abroad for everyone, regardless of whether they were members of the HVO or the BH army. So if that was the case, then there were systems that we controlled and which reflect and illustrate our behaviour and conduct. But there were also systems that we did not control, because we're talking about the following fact: What can be done, what it was possible to do, and what we wanted to do, and identity and power and this kind of thing was shown. What was feasible in a given situation and what was not feasible when the systems are controlled and not controlled, and that is the basis of what we're discussing here today when we look at documents, and we will look at the overall situation because we have to look at realistic -- the realistic situation and the objective situation. In France criminals kill. You have criminals in America, too, regardless of the fact that law and order exists and they know that this can't be done, and with all the money they have in the world they still haven't been able to reduce the crime by more than a few percent. Now I'd like to have a look at the next document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could General Praljak please slow down and give us the number of the document again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Colonel -- 3D 00635 is the number of the next document. Now, Witness, in your report, the one you sent out, you said that when I took over this family I brought in a television crew and made a spectacle out of it. Now, take a look at this next document, please. Here it says the following, briefly, that during 1992 and 1993 the hospital in Split alone, which is composed of units in Firule, Krizine, and the Spa, hospitalised 3.991 persons of Muslim nationality. And then you have the break-up according to the three localities. So the final figure is 3.991 persons who were taken care of and accommodated, and we have attached a list of all those persons giving their first and last names, and it's a document that I have, but it is in fact a Prosecution document, and my question to you is this: Did you know that we transported, paid for fuel, paid for medical assistance, that is to say the HVO and the political and military authorities and Croatian government, and with the situation we faced we did find the resources and the will to have 3.991 persons treated in just one Croatian hospital. And I'm not going to speak about the other hospitals, other places. Others will be able to address that. Did you know about that? Did you see it on CNN and on the BBC? Did you have it in your reports?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These numbers I don't have in my report and I never investigate these kind of matters. I have only one example is of the child with leukaemia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Right. Now, do you know that all the -- all the treatment for these people were free of charge or, rather, paid for by the Croatian state and that transport and everything was also calculated at a very low level [as interpreted] by Mr. Jadranko Prlic, the president of the government?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know that we discussed the matter of the child of -- with leukaemia, and we also asked ourselves how it will go further on. And the -- we got the answer that there would be no problems.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. There is something in the transcript which I simply do not quite understand. The question of Mr. Praljak is translated as --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. From the meager budget that Mr. Prlic had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Instead of "very low level," "from the meager budget." That makes sense. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, along with this document, it has 100 -- there is a list of 154 pages summarising the facts. We didn't want to burden you with 154 pages of that same material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, can you please tell us the following: Here we have in the document the localities of Firule, Krizine, and Spa. What does that mean, Firule, Krizine, and Spa?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three localities in Split, all making part and parcel of the Split hospital. The clinical hospital in Split is divided into three locality which are called Firule, Krizine and Toplice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the next document, 3D 00990, you have an entire list mentioned by the hospital in this letter, but we didn't want to burden you with 150-odd pages. We just provided one page as an illustration. But it's all in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, these lists if we find that approximately 4.000 Muslims were treated but it would have been of interest to know whether a -- Muslims civilians came in 1992, 1993, and then left, and that information does not appear on the documents. Let's imagine that civilian Muslim from Zenica was hospitalised and went back, returned to Zenica. That we can't see on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have figures from the medical files when each patient was admitted and released from hospital released from treatment for rehabilitation after treatment. But once the person is let out of the hospital, is released from the hospital and sent for rehabilitation, then the hospital no longer keeps the files. But the admission to hospital of these patients relates to 1992, 1993, and even 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Colonel, let's return to Bugojno. On the 18th of July you can see there was a conflict would you agree with me that the BH army on the 18th of July when the -- when mass was served attacked the HVO?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they attacked the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, according to the reports and to the best of your recollections, were there -- about 800 fighters of the Bugojno brigade were cut off from the road towards Gornji Vakuf, so 800 of them surrendered to the Serbs? Would that be the correct figure?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about this.
