utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: To the -- to the former question of Mr. Praljak. The question says that there was an attack when mass was served. You have not answered that element. You've just said yes, there was an attack. Do you know that there was an attack during a religious service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, no. I didn't knew that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, that's a mass. Okay. I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you, yes. We'll deal with that with a -- someone else. Now, can we note that roughly between 12 and 15.000 people at the end of July and around one and a half thousand soldiers from Bugojno start moving towards Gornji Vakuf and reached Prozor. Would that be how it was?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These numbers I'm not familiar with, but that they were gaining ground to Gornji Vakuf and Prozor, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Gerritsen, do you know that this brigade in Bugojno was made up of the local population? Their parents, brothers, sisters lived together with them. Is that something you knew about? Would you say that's correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: When this defeated army was going back, is it logical out of fear and everything else that their familiar list and friends would move along with them? That is to say the population always moves with the defeated army in retreat. Do you consider that logical?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I consider that logical, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is it true that the houses of those Croatians were set fire to? We won't say by whom, but anyway, that they were set fire to and that in many cases they were looted. According to your report would that be true?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that after that exodus and the influx of the population to Rama, to Prozor - Rama, Prozor, whichever you like to call it - that there was a complete situation of chaos? Do you agree that it was complete chaos, suggest that one can refer to as complete chaos?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the BH army wanted to the best of your knowledge take control of Makljen and move towards Prozor? Makljen as being the dominant feature of the defence of that whole area facing south?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that. That was a threat.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Would you agree with those attacks by the BH army in that particular area with greater or lesser intensity lasted throughout the month of August? Or, rather, the end of July and practically the whole of August?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that. We reported as such.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that in the night between the 1st and 2nd of August that all the HVO lines in Gornji Vakuf fell? That during the night between the 1st and 2nd of August all the lines fell in Gornji Vakuf? That the army and the people withdrew from the town and from those positions?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not familiar with these dates. I should take a look in the reports we made at that time, but I know of a certain occasion that there were a lot of fightings in Gornji Vakuf which we saw by ourselves from the location where BritBat was and where we were sleeping too, and we could see the war around us. And there was also an attack to the HQ in the barracks behind BritBat. But I was not familiar with the fact that all the lines fell in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'll try and refresh your memory. The command of the brigade -- there was a great explosion. They blew up an ammunition depot and livestock was killed and so on, and on that day they moved across Makljen. Does that refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but just a breakthrough is not a fallen of line, but that's a military discussion. It's not a fall of lines. And you fought back and regained more or less the original lines.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Colonel, can I brag a little now? Do you know that I managed to regain those lines alone on a tank, took the soldiers back with the crew of a tank and a small group, and by the evening of the 2nd of August we managed to regain our former positions? Did you hear about that? It's like sort of in the third-rate American films, but anyway, that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I was thinking of, but I -- this is the first time that I'm hearing this, that it is such a small unit that regained the lines.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I said that, after that, everyone came back in small groups and we managed to consolidate the situation later on, but we'll go into that in due course. Now look at 3D 00960, please. It's an order of mine dated the 28th of August, 1993, while the fighting was going on at great intensity. Do you remember where the villages of Pidris and Mackovac were?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know these localities, Pidris and Mackovac?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with Pidris, but I have to take a look on maps to be sure after all these years.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, that doesn't matter for now. Anyway, in my order it says that I am having people leave the area that -- where there has been a war going on for a long time, and I tell -- I say what should be done. And then I say that the livestock should be taken out with the people as well. Now, you're a professional soldier yourself. Would you consider this order to be a proper order for civilians when civilians are in an area where combat activities are going on, exposed to the danger of being collateral damage on a daily basis? Would this be the proper order to give for the villagers of these two villages? Would it be justified militarily speaking?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to look to the sentence it again -- again, so give me a few moments.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Just take your time.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, I see now, that you are giving the order to leave the area.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Children, elderly men who were not able-bodied men.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand now. Of course this is justified, in my opinion, to -- when you are sure that there will be military clashes to evacuate civilian people. But just for the time it's needed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Are you aware that as soon as the fighting died down a little they returned to their villages together with their livestock?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Please look at 3D 00741. 3D 00741. It's dated the 17th of August, 1993. Colonel, is the easiest thing to do in the army to sit down at a desk and dictate an order, say who has to do what? It's relatively easy to do that, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's relatively easy but not the way we doing that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, what I wanted to ask you was, is it sometimes futile to write orders which you know will not be complied with because the structure is not in place? And then you go and try and do other things, try to persuade people, talk to them in order to get your troops to carry out what you want? Would it be true to say that writing an order which you know there is little chance it will be complied with is -- it's better not to write such an order because it will simply undermine your authority to do that? Wouldn't that be correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a difficult question for a Dutch officer because we have a lot of orders, and -- but you are correct that sometimes you need -- it's needed that you go to the troops by yourself. But it's better to underline your orders than to have nothing on paper. But that depends -- all depends on the time you have. The more time you have, the more paper you have. And I do not know how much time you had at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, you know how little sleep we were able to snatch, but on the 17th of August, when I learned that prisoners were being taken to dig trenches, I issued an order. Later on there was a general order applicable to the whole of the HVO saying that this must not be done. But let me ask you the following: Are you aware that after the date on which this order of mine was issued there was a far smaller number of those who dared to take prisoners out to dig trenches? Are you aware that after the 17th of August there was a significant reduction in the number of those who in various ways took prisoners to dig?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that because we were in the position to do fairly specific investigations on this matter. We couldn't count. We couldn't travel everywhere because of mines and because of our safety. So this is -- I cannot -- I can't confirm.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's look at 3D 00967. It's dated the 31st of July, 1993, and in this document I issue an order saying how the troops under my command should behave towards UNPROFOR units, humanitarian aid convoys, and so on. Can you confirm that the route for humanitarian aid was always open except when there was fierce fighting nearby, Pidris, Mackovac, Makljen, and so on, that it was always possible except when there was very heavy fighting going on?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In one of your reports you wrote that, "One week seven helicopters flew to the hospital in Rumboci," and then you said you expected the same in the following week. Apart from the HVO having a hospital in Rumboci near Prozor, every day I had to take the seriously wounded by helicopter. Do you know what number of HVO men were killed or wounded in the fighting around Gornji Vakuf in that period?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I would like to move on to another document. Your Honours, I was given 25 minutes by Mr. Ibrisimovic, so please count this into my time. I have some more documents to put to the witness, if I may. Please look at P 05162. This is a report written by you, dated the 17th of September, 1993, where you speak about the general situation. You say that in Gornji Vakuf there was fierce fighting in the early morning, that the Diamond route was still open. But let's look at what it says about the political situation. The population in Prozor is quiet -- or, rather, receive the Uzdol massacre quietly, and so far there has been no maltreatment of the Muslim community. And on the next page it says, "Violence against the Muslim massacre in Prozor which we first expected. As yet it has not happened." You know what happened in Uzdol; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, where are we supposed to find this document, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P 05 -- it's Watkins --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's a Prosecution document but it's on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's my fault. It's Watkins -- I'm sorry, I'll refer to it -- oh, it's on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you know about the Uzdol massacre?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Colonel, are you aware that even after the Uzdol massacre, either on the 17th or later on, there was no retaliation against the Muslim population in Prozor? Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there at that time because I left after Uzdol to Tomislavgrad. From there I was interested in what was going on in Gornji Vakuf and surroundings. And I read the reports from Gornji Vakuf, and I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: But Tomislavgrad was not far from Rama. Did you hear in any report that there was any kind of retaliation against the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Are you aware that I put the imam under guard in order to protect him from the possible consequences of such an event? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: From what you wrote about the war, when 10 per cent of the villagers, and more than 10 per cent of a small village are massacred, can you resolve such a situation by writing an order or by numbers of meetings where you have to beg, shout, plead, discuss, persuade? I was an officer. Is it enough to write an order or is there much more that one has to do in order to prevent a relative, a brother, a sister to take revenge?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course you need much more.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We would now -- could we see the film about Uzdol now to see what happened there? It's four minutes, so let's look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Your Honours, before we do show it, I'm just wondering, I mean, is this relevant to the -- again, is this relevant to the indictment? Uzdol is not part of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Flynn speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's not relevant to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you're going to play a video about Uzdol. What is the purpose of this? What do you want to establish?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, please. First of all, it's Prozor municipality. Secondly, in my view it's quite logical and correct to allow Your Honours to assess my guilt when you see what any commander can possibly do after a massacre of this kind in a place where there are 10 to 15.000 refugees. What is it possible to do, because the Prosecution keeps saying that there was absolute and total control. But if you don't know this -- it's Prozor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, also we can see the witness on the film, and the witness said he was in Uzdol, and it is relevant to command and control quite clearly. This circumstance has been mentioned in questions, so let a soldier tell us whether under certain circumstances it's possible to control the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... minutes we'll play the video. It's only four minutes. We'll play the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours -- excuse me --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the Witness -- there was a witness there who said nothing happened in Uzdol.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, but, I mean, Mr. Praljak goes on and other people have gotten up and spoke, and I understand it's a question that -- it may only take four minutes, but again, it's -- there's a broader principle here. This illustrates the point the Prosecution made earlier this afternoon. The event at Uzdol is not disputed. It's not disputed. There's no point in showing something about it, except that, I put it, it's just simply to show pictures to the Chamber that -- I mean, I'm sure are very unfortunate. I'm sure what happened there is very unfortunate, but it has no value to the case as such and otherwise, Your Honour, we can do this all day long. People can come in and show their videos and it has no relevance at all to the issues in the case. We don't dispute that Uzdol happened. If it's not disputed why are we trying to prove something that's not disputed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may briefly assist in the matter. At some point you will need to address on issues related to command responsibility under 7.3. As General Praljak has been indicating that the situation was rather tense, we have a massacre there, and then the situation is can a commander under those circumstances, in light of the -- all the people that he has under his command, can he control every individual, and it goes to the issue of effective command and control, and I think that -- and I think that this is relevant because, as it was pointed out by General Praljak, you have family members there. You have all sorts of people. This was a citizens' army. So I think it goes to the very heart of -- of that issue. So that's why it's necessary to look at the film. And I think it also -- as was indicated, we had a witness who -- from an international organisation who simply denied the existence of this incident and wrote a report about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well, let's see the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Voiceover: "... poor for a different morning. The division of Bosnia proposed in the Geneva peace talks gave the Muslims 30 per cent of the land, an offer they [indiscernible]. Since the peace talks floundered, the Muslim forces have continued their offensive in Central Bosnia and have taken more territory by force. The massacre took place at Uzdol, 40 miles west of Sarajevo after Croat soldiers failed to hold the village and it was taken by the Muslim Bosnian army. You may find some of the pictures in this report disturbing. "The village of Uzdol is high in the hills of Central Bosnia. It has a school building, lately used as a local Croat military headquarters. Yesterday, the Bosnian army descended on Uzdol then withdrew leaving terrible evidence of their brief visit. "We walked through the scattered farms and cottages with British soldiers and European Monitors trying to establish what happened here. It soon became clear that every house and cottage had been visited by the Bosnian army soldiers. Systematic slaughter. Every room had been entered. There were bullets in the bedroom walls. An old lady killed in her bed. The victims times were all elderly, and one child unable to flee. Some had tried to hide. One couple, 67-year-old Martin Ratkic and his wife Kara had taken refuge in their barn. They lay in each other's arms, apparently shot by someone standing over them. "The word 'atrocity' has been used a lot in this war. It's usually very difficult to find out exactly what has happened. There is so much propaganda and myth, but in this case it seems clear that there was wholesale killing of civilians, but as to the reason it's a-almost impossible for an observer to guess. One answer came from a Croat soldier who came back to his family house to find his mother burned in the ruins. "'It is a war. It is a war,' he said. They hate civilians. They hate us.' For the UN, in this instance British soldiers and the European Monitors, there is nothing they can do except to observe and report to a European committee. "Probably they would say maybe it's a wartime because they slaughter civilians, and maybe in the future there will be an investigation of the court of justice in The Hague or something like that. "22 of the victims had already been taken to a makeshift morgue in the nearby town of Prozor. Again the UN and the EC observed and did not comment, very conscious of the way such incidents in this war are either distorted or denied, becoming part of the propaganda of both sides, with the UN being seen as a convenient scapegoat. Such was the nature of the killing at Uzdol that recriminations have not yet gathered force and grief was only beginning. "Kate Adie, BBC news. Uzdol. "Inflation rose in August by ..."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Colonel, did you recognise yourself a little younger in this footage?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Are you aware that there were soldiers from this village who were in the Rama Brigade, so that these were their parents, sisters, and so on, because men from Uzdol were part of the Rama HVO Brigade. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Are you aware that only two days later, on the 16th of September, in the same municipality, Prozor, in the village of Hudotsko, 24 civilians who were of Croat ethnicity were killed?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's new for me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. You were still there before you left in September 1993. I'm referring to 3D 00942. It's a document I have already shown, but it was not -- it had not all been translated then. It is a diary kept by a journalist about operation Neretva 93. Colonel, are you aware that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the 13th of September, 1993, started or launched operation Neretva 93 from the north with a view to coming to the western borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina? So the attack went from Vakuf towards Mostar on all axes, Jablanica, Mostar. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These kind of specific information we haven't had it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In that case, I'll just put one more question. The operation was launched on the 13th, but you were still there, and it says here at Crni Vrh, which is at Makljen, was on fire. It was a flame from detonations and infantry fighting. Did you know that on the 13th Crni Vrh and the area around it was on fire because of the detonations?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's not mentioned in our daily report, we were not aware of that. I have to look in my daily report, because this is typical military information, and normally we will report such things.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I did not find anything except that there was fighting, although in this book it says Commander Karic, Vehbija Karic and Rifat Bilajic were washing their feet in the stream, and they said, "We had our shoes on for three days." Do you know that the fighting went on continually from the 13th to the 17th, 24 hours a day, round the clock? If not, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Let me ask you this, Colonel: Is it correct that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had two tanks in -- in Vakuf which they had taken from the HVO in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember such thing, but I must say vaguely.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. A lot of time has gone by. It's quite understandable. Are you aware, and my commanders kept saying this to BritBat, that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the part of down under their control, 30 metres behind the BritBat it held mortar positions and fired from them? Did the British complain to you that the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina had mortar positions right next to their base?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't, they -- complain to me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: That was when I was referring to -- when I said that somebody told them five minutes before HVO artillery would shoot that they should take cover, because we kept telling them that they should remove the mortars from a built-up area. Do you know that the mortars of Bosnia-Herzegovina were among the local population in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We didn't count them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please give us how much time is left?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Colonel, are you aware that units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina fired at the HVO from houses inhabited by civilians? In Gornji Vakuf, in the part under the control of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Very often they opened fire on HVO units from houses in which there were civilians.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of that. I have seen that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Let me just see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've used one hour and five minutes so far, and the registrar informed me that you have 20 more minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that just my time? Because this lady, Mrs. Alaburic, is -- follows me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Ms. Alaburic, how much time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can give five or 10 minutes to General Praljak if he needs it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But yourself need?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I give him 10 minutes, I will then take only 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So at this point the Prosecution, will they have any additional questions? Will the Prosecution have any additional questions at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I will have a number of questions. I hope they will be short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Colonel, in one of your reports you mention the fact that the BH army had helicopters and that it used the helicopters to transport many of its deputies to some Assembly. Do you know that, while you were in Gornji Vakuf, did indeed have helicopters?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not -- I do not remember. In my opinion, there were no helicopters when I was in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I didn't mean in Gornji Vakuf. What I actually meant was that in Zenica, that they had helicopters in Zenica, for example. And in the book that I mentioned, a pilot tells a journalist that he had 500 sorties for the BH army. Did you have facts and figures of that kind? Did you know about things like that?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In a document, which I have no reason to doubt, it's your report, actually, you say that Alagic, General Alagic, the commander of the BH army, said the following about the cleansing in the Lasva Valley: "The BH army is not in a hurry --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you kindly tell us which document you are referring to so that we can follow, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to P 03771. I'm referring to document P 03771.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And in that document in inverted commas General Alagic's words are quoted in response to a question about the intentions the BH army, and he says in quotation marks: "We're not in a hurry to cleanse the remaining Croatian areas," and he means by that the Lasva River valley. Now do you know this position, that when they had taken control of the surrounding parts they considered that they could finish off with the Lasva River valley subsequently, and that they would set a time for doing this. So do you know about this about General Alagic and what their plans were with respect to the Lasva River valley?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This isn't a report from me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It's an observer a European observer, I don't think it was but you I just wanted to know if you were aware of this from your talks and reading documents or anything?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'd like to refer to the following document P 03944, dated the 4th of August, 1993, by the European Monitors, European observers, and in that document mention is made of an offensive by the BH army --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's an ECMM document. Out of an abundance of caution I don't think it should be made public outside the courtroom. My colleague -- well, my colleague has told me that the necessary has already been done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, in document P 03944 dated the 4th of August, 1993, the ECMM speaks about a BH army offensive from Travnik towards Bugojno, Gornji Vakuf, Rama, et cetera. Did you know of these intentions for an offensive and the plans of the BH army along these lines?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In document P 04363, P 04363, dated the 20th of August, 1993, mention is made of the following: "The BH army is not allowing the evacuation from Nova Bila to take place by helicopter of the wounded," the HVO wounded, because, it says, "the HVO is bringing in ammunition." Do you know that the BH army did not allow the evacuation of the wounded to take place from Nova Bila with HVO helicopters and the Nova Bila hospital in the Lasva River valley?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know of what happened in Vrbas Valley. This kind of thing, Nova Bila, I have heard of but not witnessed in one way or another. There were all kind of negotiations going on about evacuations exchanges, but it always took time before we got an agreement with all the parties involved. But Lasva Valley, I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In document P 4535 that I'd like to refer to of the 26th of August, 1993, it says in point 2 -- or, rather, point 3 that the transport of delegates, 90 Bosnian Herzegovinian delegates, Muslims, from Zenica to Sarajevo, was performed despite the flight ban. Do you know that these 50 persons -- or 90 persons were transported by helicopter on this date, the 26th of August, to an Assembly of the Party of Democratic Action or whatever? Do you know about that, despite the no-fly ban?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Praljak. Can you enlighten the Chamber on the relevance of this? I can't make any link with the indictment or any other matter, actually.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'll explain right away, Judge Trechsel. In a report by the colonel, it says that the Muslims in Gornji Vakuf were complaining terribly about two things. First, that the water supply for Bugojno had been shut off -- cut off, and, secondly, that they had no diesel fuel and that was the reason they couldn't transport their wounded to the hospital in Bugojno. What I want to show with this is the BH army, as I showed with the previous document, received fuel regularly and used it to fuel the tanks and helicopter flights, and it told the European Monitors that they didn't even have 200 litres of diesel fuel to be able to transport their wounded to Bugojno, pulling the wool over their eyes. So that was my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: If they knew there were that many flights and helicopter and tank movements then my question to you Colonel is whether the military authorities of the BH army in Gornji Vakuf complained that they didn't even have 200 litres of fuel to transport the wounded to Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I have to answer now? I know of the diesel and that by a kind of -- such reasons it was not possible to bring out the wounded. So that's what we did. We brought diesel to that hospital. And of course I have opinion about that, and -- well, it's a matter of -- in my case it was a matter of humanitarian aid. It wasn't important for me if they had it or had it not. We only try to get the wounded out. And I think 200 litre is not much. But I do not know the exact situation from the ABiH, of course, but it's not likely that they hadn't diesel at all. It is more likely that it was difficult to bring the diesel to the hospital in Kalin hotel, in the Kalin hotel. Maybe that was a problem.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Now, I'm not sorry that you provided the fuel to save the wounded, Colonel. My next question -- one or two more questions and then I'll be finished, and my penultimate question is this: If I were to put map before you if you can remember where was it in your opinion that the HVO who held certain lines -- which held certain lines around Gornji Vakuf, where - in what locality - could it have cut off the water supply for Bugojno? Did you know that then? Did you find it out later on? What place was it possible for them to do this? Where could the HVO, in the places it was in control of, could it have cut off the water supply for Bugojno, which is 19 kilometres away?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not familiar with all waterlines in Bugojno and surroundings. You have to be on the spot. That's the only thing I know, and I can't say whether or not it was possible here in this room.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: When they told you that the HVO had cut off the water supply somewhere, were you certain then or did you just convey that information in your report without checking to see where this could have happened, where it was possible for the HVO to cut off the water supply? Did you do that? Did you investigate the matter or did you just send the information further on through your report without checking yourself?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't check it. We just sent it further on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. And my last question: Witness, as far as I remember, we met several times. Once we talked with two other BritBat officers present, I believe. I prefer facts rather than opinions and impressions. Tell me, was I ready to let you go where you wanted to go, to answer your questions, to give my views, unofficially and in an open, frank conversation without trying to hide any information or anything like that? Is that the impression you gained after your meeting with me, for instance?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the impression, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Colonel, thank you for answering my questions. Thank you for coming to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that completes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will take a 20-minute break, and we shall start in 20 minutes' time from now, and Ms. Alaburic will start the cross-examination. Completes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before my colleague starts, perhaps this is a good time for me to ask for an IC number for the video at Uzdol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the video will become IC 587.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel Gerritsen, good afternoon to you. I have very little time at my disposal, and I'd like to make the best use of it possible to the benefit of all in the courtroom. Therefore I'd like to ask you that you with your great military knowledge and experience throw light on some relevant events. To start off with, I'd like to refer to my colleague, Mr. Kovacic, Defence counsel for General Praljak, who asked you questions about the possibility or impossibility of effective control, and in that context I'd like to draw your attention, to begin with, to one single document that I have prepared for your testimony. I don't know if it has been given to the witness. P 09672, and it is a report by the European Monitors dated the 14th of October, 1993, and what I would like to discuss with you refers to point 8. But before that, can we just take note that the report was compiled in Tomislavgrad. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And you were still in Tomislavgrad yourself, because at the beginning we hear that you will be leaving in the following week. That's what it says at the very beginning, in the second portion.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Colonel, did you see this report before? Did you see it before or is this the first time you have it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had such -- such reports in Tomislavgrad.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, in point 8 mention is made of the HVO, and it says that the 5th Army [as interpreted] is still weak, although it is under the control of the state. The process of its organisation has still not been completed. It is being established by the municipalities and the state. And when in November 1992 the head of the Bosnian Croat government was moved to Mostar or, rather, Grude, the brigades were placed directly under its command, which led to the establishment of the operative zones. Now, Mr. Gerritsen, can we discuss the HVO as an army and how this was assessed by your institution, that is to say an army in its inception, in the process of being established? Can you confirm or deny whether the HVO was really as it is described here? And before --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I can confirm that. An army should have, for instance, uniforms, and of course all the same. It's all written down in the Geneva Conventions. And regarding the -- regarding the Geneva Conventions, HVO was a regular army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I interject, with your leave, a question on this sentence? It says: "The army is under state control." Which state is referred to here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The state of -- what's the name? I remember names as Mate Boban and -- I do not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: He was not a state.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How should I call this state?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Colonel --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... But.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Colonel, are you thinking of the state which at that point in time was called the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna? Are you thinking of Herceg-Bosna? Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Herceg-Bosna, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I didn't put a leading question. I very carefully avoided it. Thank you. Excuse me, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All these names.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to put the transcript correct. On page 70, line 15, it says "the 5th Army," where it should be the HVO. So we're just referring to the HVO. Now, Colonel, do you know that the HVO was formed from the military units which had been established at the level of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: From this report that we read out it would follow that in November 1992 the Main Staff a started taking over control over those municipal units, because it says when in November 1992 the headquarters of the government was moved, the brigades were placed under the command of the Main Staff. Now, do you know that at the end of 1992 the Main Staff started taking over control of the municipal military units? Is that something you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I haven't dates in my memory of these -- of these kind of events, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you then explain to us this date November 1992, which is mentioned item 8 of the report?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a report. I confirmed this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat the question. So can you confirm that at the end of 1992, as it says in the report, in November the Main Staff of the HVO started taking over control over the municipal military units?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this way I can confirm this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Colonel, to the best of your knowledge what is the usual time necessary when a decision is made that somebody would start taking over control over the military units in a certain area? For example, how much time is realistically necessary for that control to take effect, for them to take over control? I know it's a general question, but on the basis your knowledge or the examples of the Dutch army, can you perhaps tell us, or is it enough to make the decision in written form and that solves the problem?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it takes -- it takes time. The question is how much. I think that event in 1992 makes the HVO army -- from that moment on you have an army. If it is weak or -- whatsoever or not well-organised, but it's a big risk to fight at the same moment. You need training and so on. It depends on the situation, if you start fighting at the moment, but it's great risk. It depends on what the enemy does. But it's not a regular army as we have at this moment. That takes years. It's also a matter of culture, and that takes years to teach and to have the same behaviour. Yeah, years. Maybe to have an army like the Croatian army had at the end of the war, or the Dutch army at this moment, well, ten years or more. But you can also say that you have to do -- you have to do it with the means you have, and this army had not the means but also the ABiH not so. So it was in one way or the other equal. So that reduces the risk in terms of winning or not winning. In terms of fights, as the Geneva Conventions describes, I think it's not possible, but it's -- that is stated already once this afternoon. It's very difficult, and there are great risks. I already agreed with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we analyse item 8, especially in the portion where it says that the HVO army is financed by the municipalities and the state? Now, based on your military experience and knowledge, could we conclude then that if a municipality finances its military unit or, rather, the military unit located in its area, will the power -- will the authorities in that municipality affect the conduct of that military unit or the actions of that military unit?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand it well, it is always difficult when you get a new commander to obey for hundred per cent. That takes time. You need confidence for the new situation. Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, no, not really. I was thinking about the possibility of wielding influence, the local authorities wielding influence on military units in the area with respect to control and command from a state level, a higher level. Is the -- is there the possibility of intervening from the aspects of the local authority financing the local military unit? Based on your experience as a soldier, would you expect that logically? But if you don't have any experience with that, we can move on.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a couple of hundred years ago, I think, we had the same problem in the Dutch army. That's a bit a problem. Of course you have problems with that. That's obvious for me, but just as a logical human, I think that, but I have no experience with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's now discuss some matters which you'll find easier to discuss. You were in the area of responsibility of Bugojno, Gornji Vakuf, and Prozor from mid-July to mid-September 1993. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Is that area considered to be a territorial whole in the sense that the events in Bugojno reflect upon the situation and events in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about the fact that in any of these places in that area events there would reflect the state of relations in Central Bosnia or, for example, the Mostar region?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specific, but it has, of course, reflections.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, a number two, the Bugojno question. You told us in your statement -- it says that the BH army had taken control of Bugojno, and in the statement you gave to the Prosecution of this Tribunal in connection with another trial, the proceedings against Hadzihasanovic and Kubura, you spoke, among other things, about the fact that the Croatian prisoners of war were beaten, that there were houses that had been set on fire, that the BH army set fire to houses as well, and that the Croatian civilians were exposed to looting, threats, and attacks. And these observations are reflected in your reports, too. I have the numbers of those reports, but perhaps we can summarise it in one question: Do you remember those portions of your reports? Do you know what I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In one of your reports for the 13th of August, and it is P 9631, point 2(C) for those who would like to look this up, it was concluded that the Croatian Community lives in fear. And in another document, also for Their Honours the number is 9656, it is the report for the 1st of August, point 4, you state that the Croats in Bugojno were concerned for their future. Colonel, on the basis of these reports of yours, would it be well-founded to conclude that fear on the part of the Croatian community in Bugojno was realistic, a realistic fear?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a realistic fear, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge to the effect that, with respect to this situation in the Croatian Community in Bugojno, the inhabitants of other places in Bosnia and Herzegovina which had Croatian populations were aware of this?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If we could clarify the part of your report that deals with the prisoners in the secondary school in Prozor. In document P 9650, referring to the 9th of July, which is before your arrival, so I'll ask you if you know of this, it says that Colonel Siljeg told the observers -- or, rather, the monitors of the European Community that they could go to the school. He made it possible for them to go to the school. They could see that the prisoners were being treated well. So did you know that the European Monitors were the first to be granted permission to visit the prisoners in the school?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the courtroom, Colonel, we have had witnesses testifying about the way the detainees were being treated in the school. We were also able to see a logbook of the events. So I wish to ask you whether you were aware of some of these facts. For example, did you know that the detainees were able to go home to wash, to change, sometimes spend the night at home, that --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which detainees and when?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The detainees in Prozor in the technical school in the summer of 1993, that they were able to go home for the summer harvest without ever being escorted either by a soldier or military policeman of the HVO, that they all always returned to the school, that none of them ever escaped? Were you aware of these details about the treatment of the detainees in the school?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told us, yes, when we visited them once. The harvest I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Were you told that they could be visited by members of their family who could bring them food?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember such.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Were you told that they went to work in various locations that had nothing to do with any wartime events? For example, in bakeries, a warehouse, a motel, a petrol station, and so on. And that in many of these places the food was better than it was in detention.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that it was precisely because of this that many of the detainees reported voluntarily to go to work in one of places I have mentioned?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the school was guarded only by two home guards at a time?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that none of the Muslims ever escaped or tried to run away from the school?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Colonel, in your statement tendered into evidence on page 10 of the text in English, in the last passage you say that on the 26th of August, 1993, you reported seeing 25 prisoners of war of Muslim ethnicity used by the HVO to dig trenches. As it is not in doubt that various categories of people were being detained, I wish to ask you how you established that these were prisoners of war and that they were members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the -- the date is the 26th, but the date of the imprisoned people before this. What was exactly the date?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there seems to be an error, Ms. Alaburic. Perhaps the translation. You speak of prisoners of war of Muslim ethnicity used by the HVO to dig trenches, and then you say, "How did you establish that these were prisoners of war and that they were members of the --" oh, a short while ago it still read HVO. It has been corrected in the meantime. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We visited the technical school at a certain date, and from the technical school people dig trenches. We also visited other detainees in Prozor who were in better is circumstances than in the technical school. That is what I remember. So now I'm confused about which detainees we are speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We can jog your memory and remind you of your statement. I quoted you correctly. I assume you still have it before you in the Prosecution's set of documents, but perhaps we don't need to spend time on that. We had prisoners of war. We had civilians. We had another category who were members of the HVO who had been disarmed. So I wish to know how you established that these particular people were prisoners of war rather than civilians or some third category of detainees.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, that's difficult. It's mixed up. For sure is that not every detainee was a soldier, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I think it would be very useful if you were to clarify to us a military term which we lawyers perhaps often misinterpret or fail to understand. Today, when General Praljak asked you about Alagic's book, he quoted his words saying, "We are not in a hurry to cleanse the remaining Croatian area." In your report referring to the 2nd of August, 1993, and it's in the Prosecution set of documents, D9657.3, you said, "As reported last night the Bosnia-Herzegovina side launched a large-scale attack last night in the Gornji Vakuf area. They achieved most of their goals, but there had still -- there are still small groups of HVO moving through the area. The Bosnian-Herzegovinian forces are still mopping up or cleansing the terrain." Colonel, can you tell us what to "mop up" or "cleanse the terrain" means in military terms?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That you remove all the elements which normally are being called enemies. You take them in prison, or if that's not possible and there are fightings, you can wound them or kill them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If I may put a subquestion. Does that mean that after fierce fighting you go back to the battlefield and check it to see whether in a ruined house, for example, or somewhere else an enemy's still hiding?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's a normal procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have concluded. Thank you. Colonel, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, before I give the floor to the Prosecution for final examination I have a question myself. We have watched a video submitted by General Praljak, and we saw you in that footage. You were there in Uzdol, and obviously you were not aware of Neretva 1993 operation. Did you know that two days before -- a few days before Uzdol, Grabovica had taken place? Were you aware of the massacre that occurred in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, later; not at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, when you went to Uzdol, you did not know that a few days before that time there had been a massacre perpetrated where 33 persons had been killed in Grabovica? Nobody had told you about it?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We hadn't -- we had not that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We saw you in that video, but we also saw a number of soldiers from the HVO apparently, because they were carrying weapons, wearing camouflage uniforms. So we can come to the conclusion that there were members of the HVO and not the ABiH. I also noticed a soldier with blue berets, probably someone from UNPROFOR. When you were there on site, in theatre, did no one wonder who had committed these crimes?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we wonder, and the most likely conclusion at that moment was the ABiH. Because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm looking at the way -- what I said was translated, and I had said who had done this, and in English it had been translated as who had committed these crimes. That's not what I intended to say. I wanted to say who had done this, and it was a very general sentence. I would like to ask the interpreters to be extremely accurate when they translate what I say because French is an extremely accurate language, and it's not -- should not be interpreted any which way because then it has dramatic consequences.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or a lot of consequences, interpreter's corrections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So let me come back to my question. Your conclusion was that it was the ABiH, but did you know why, what was the objective, what it was related to?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the question what the objective could be, and one of the objectives could be - we talked about that - revenge or have fear among -- to get fear among the population. ABiH was in the -- was in the surrounding of Uzdol. They -- it took not long to be -- to get at Uzdol. More I can't say. These are just suggestions. We weren't sure about anything, because we only saw that people, and -- and we had to draw conclusions by the stories we've got from the people who were there, and that were people from, as you said, from the HVO and the mayor of Prozor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a representative of the European Union, because you were a monitor on behalf of Europe, didn't it occur to you to go and see the ABiH to ask them for explanations?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Under these circumstances -- circumstances, we always do that, ask for explanations. But the problem for me personally was that at the same day I went to Tomislavgrad. In the morning I witness it, Uzdol, because I was there, and in the afternoon I had to go to Tomislavgrad. It was a coincidence that it was on the same day. And I'm not aware of what Dave MacIver, my successor, did in this case. That's a strange coincidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. One last, very brief question. You were a monitor, an observer as part of this European mission, and one of your duties, one of the municipalities in your area of responsibility was Prozor. So theoretically you should have been aware of everything that was going on, on both sides, on the HVO side and on the ABiH side. So at no point were you -- were you aware that there might be an action by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the case of Uzdol, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I -- you mean in advance. That's why the answer is no. In advance, we didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the task of a monitor is to anticipate events, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. If we expect something, we go to a specific place to investigate. When there are -- fighting going on, we went there. We -- that's the way we were working. I agree. But not in the case of Uzdol. We didn't get in advance any evidences that there would be a massacre on the -- in Uzdol, or fightings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Flynn.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Lieutenant Colonel. I have a very -- a few short questions for you. My first question is relative to the exhibit which I showed to you yesterday, 0P 6 -- 0P 9636 in the booklet, the Prosecution booklet. Before I ask you the question, as I see it from the transcript, yesterday what you told us towards the end of the day was that in or around the 10th of August of 1993, you learned from the imam in Prozor that the Muslim population had been gathered up and moved somewhere on the east side. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And then a number of days later, specifically, I think, on the 19th of August when you visited POWs in Prozor in the school, you got information -- or afterwards you got information that the Muslims were actually rounded up and put in three separate locations, Podgrade, Lapsunj, and Duge. Am I correct so far?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And a few days after that you learned some disturbing news from the imam that the Muslims bow in these places had been moved?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And this brought us to the 1st of September when you had a meeting with Colonel Zeljko Siljeg, which you referred to in your report to the 1st of September, Exhibit P 636, and your evidence was that Colonel Siljeg had told you that they had gone to Muslim territory and had gone voluntarily. Correct so far?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And then Ms. Tomasegovic, when she was questioning you yesterday, referred you to this exhibit, and then she said to you that from reading the exhibit what she deduces is that the movement to Jablanica and to Konjic, the Muslim areas, was something that you had not discussed but that you had discussed their moving to Podgrade and Lapsunj, and she said, "Am I right in saying that?" And you agreed with her that -- you agreed with what she said. I just for clarification want to know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Flynn.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Flynn, please stop. Ms. Tomasegovic doesn't seem to be agreeing with you. She's on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't agree, because I think that Mr. Flynn is quoting what I said erroneously. I put it to the witness what it says in the document, and that was Jablanica and Konjic that is mentioned, and I read out the sentence word-for-word as it stands in the document. Now, as far as Podgrade and Duge is concerned, this is something mentioned by the witness in response to a question from my learned colleague when the colleague asked him on the basis of which he's able to conclude -- on the basis of what is he able to conclude that Colonel Siljeg did not -- was not telling the truth when he said that it was voluntary departure. Then this witness here in his statement said, in court, that he concluded that from talking to people who were moved to Podgrade and Duge. And I just pointed out the logical conclusion, that he talked to people who found themselves in Podgrade and Duge where they were isolated, and not in talking to people who had gone to Jablanica and Konjic because he didn't find anybody there either when they moved or -- nor was he in Jablanica and Konjic. And he told us himself that he didn't even know under whose control Jablanica and Konjic were nor did he have anything to do with that area. So what I'm saying now is what the witness said on page 72 of yesterday's transcript, lines 8 to 13, and I even referred to part of the transcript where he mentioned Podgrade and Duge. And if my colleague is quoting me, would he quote me correctly, because these are not minor mistakes. They're mistakes which essentially change what I said and what the witness said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And I will quote the -- what was said. I drew it from the transcript which had been corrected and which appears on page 1924, and it says from line 14 where you were -- where you're discussing -- there's the mention of a discussion with Colonel Siljeg, and it says: "However, from this document," referring to the report, "we can see that it wasn't the fact that the Muslims were moved from Lapsunj and Podgrade but from Jablanica and Konjic. And from that I deduce from this movement to Jablanica and Konjic was not something you had discussed. You had discussed their moving to Podgrade and Lapsunj. Am I right in saying that?"

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And, Colonel, your reply was: "I agree with you so far." Now, I only raise the matter because earlier you had told us that at the meeting with Colonel Siljeg you had actually discussed the movement of the Muslims to the Muslim territory. So I'm wondering, was the conversation a discussion on the movement of Muslims to Muslim territory or was the discussion on the movement of the Muslims from parts of Prozor to the east of Prozor, namely the three locations that you had mentioned earlier? It's just a matter of clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think I heard it correctly and in the transcript it says that the colleague was quoting this from 1924, page 1924.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the witness can tell us. Colonel, you heard the exchange. You heard the question put to you by Mr. Flynn. Can you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. If I'm correct, what -- I should go into the files, but we discuss with Siljeg also the -- the moment that the Muslims who were in Podgrade and Duge and Lapsunj were left to other territory, Jablanica and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this morning when Mr. Kovacic was questioning you, the issue of impartiality arose, and to paraphrase it, effectively you told the -- the Trial Chamber that in your opinion some of your colleagues may have been more in favour of the Muslims. What I want to ask you is this: The daily reports which emanated from your area, Gornji Vakuf, were they balanced reports or were they slanted in favour of one side or the other?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think overall the conclusion is -- must be that these were balanced reports. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you show any partiality to one side or the other when drafting the reports?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Discussions I saw only -- I saw partiality.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: But the reports that finally issued and went to Zenica, did they represent the true position on the ground?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They present the true position on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: You're happy with that?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm happy with that. We had a discussion. I didn't -- I -- I can't say -- well, these are slight differences, you know, but these are balanced reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, just moving on to a different topic. Again Mr. Kovacic and General Praljak mentioned -- or questioned you in relation to responsibilities of the military leaders and the question of -- of what you would expect officers -- the duties and responsibilities of officers under the circumstances that you found yourself, and particularly given the nature of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I think you said that it was not possible to persuade all men under the command of a senior officer to -- to comply according to the Geneva Convention; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. There are risks, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: But when you brought complaints to senior officers, would you have expected those officers to make at least some effort to correct the situation, any infractions that you made complaints about?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And your testimony yesterday, you indicated that you complained on numerous occasions, whether it be about forced labour or other infractions. And did you see any effort on the part of the HVO at any stage to correct these infractions?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw till the end of my stage in that area people digging trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And all the way up to the time you left?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not -- yes, till the end. It's -- not the last day, of course. I -- but till the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And you spoke --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Yes, Ms. Tomasegovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I feel called upon personally with respect to part of the transcript read out by my colleague Mr. Flynn because he was selective in reading out part of the transcript and not the introductory couple of sentences, which confirmed precisely what I said here a few minutes ago. With the Court's permission, I'd like to read out the first three sentences so that he can see that I'm not insinuating anything but that I quoted the transcript to the best of my recollections at -- precisely as it was said and recorded in the transcript. And I'm going to read out the introductory part and then come to the portion of the quotation that was read out by Mr. Flynn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... necessary because we can certainly read it ourselves. Very well. Mr. Flynn, please put your question and we will see.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Not so long ago you were answering questions from Ms. Alaburic about the formation of the HVO, around you were talking about a young army, and that it wasn't a regular army. And given that it would take time for the HVO to effectively put itself together and become a regular army as you would know a regular army, would you expect senior commanders to be more careful about the orders which they gave?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. When you expect certain risks, you have to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And you fairly mentioned -- you fairly replied to General Praljak when he asked you was it enough just to write an order and expect somebody to comply with an order, and you said no. What steps would an officer be expected to take to see that an order was followed up?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, control, of course, reports, investigations, all these type of things. You can visit the units by yourself and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And would you expect an officer, if he found his orders weren't being followed, to take disciplinary action against those people not performing their duties?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You try to take measures. The question is always did you have punish people or you can also teach people. But there are certain things that shouldn't happen, and the question is always: Does the soldier in question knows about all these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection to make with respect to Mr. Flynn's question. It is this: I think that we ought to be more precise in defining the time to which the question relates with respect to the conduct of commanders, because in situations of war priorities are different from what they are in peacetime. So may we be precise on this point? Is he talking about situations when there is shelling in town, intensive fighting, or are we talking about relatively peaceful periods?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I'm talking about the circumstances under which the HVO were formed, established themselves, and conducted their activities, and I'm wondering -- my question is directed in relation of the HVO from their formation onwards. So you're talking about 1992, 1993, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I would support my colleague, Ms. Alaburic. That is too general. The objection which Ms. Alaburic raised was very specific. In what circumstances? The witness provided a general response, and we agree with it. The issue is, however, whether the priorities are change while we are in -- directly involved in fighting or we are out of the fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And I may ask that question once I get an answer to my general question, but I'm leading into it, and if you would allow me to do so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Flynn. The question that you put is a legal question in nature, because it is -- it concerns the disciplinary power of commanders, of superiors. So you can put the question on the way it goes in the Dutch army in peacetime and in war times, and then you can also ask the witness if he can make a comparison with what he may have seen within the HVO. But to ask him directly to find out how the disciplinary measures are taken in the HVO, to me it seems a very hazardous thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, this witness was asked specifically about his impressions of the HVO by Ms. Alaburic, and he gave his impressions, and there was no objection from the Prosecution, and the Bench didn't object to it either. I'm moving -- I'm continuing that subject and that discussion. He was on the ground. He was in a position to see what was going on with the HVO, and I believe he would be in a position to answer the question whether or not -- from what he saw, whether the senior officers should have followed up with disciplinary actions if they saw that their junior officers were not carrying out their duties. I don't see anything wrong with the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Can you answer that question, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Which question should I answer now?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, we'll be more specific. We were talking about the HVO, and we had discussed the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please, Mr. Flynn. In order not to waste any time to the Trial Chamber, when we talk about Article 7(3), you know there is a division. The responsible must take preventive measures. The responsible also has to have knowledge and must sanction. So there are steps. It's quite complicated. The witness -- does the witness know this? I would be very surprised. You can of course put him a general question to that effect and to ask us to give us his assessment, to tell us what superiors did within the HVO and how they've carried out disciplinary actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Colonel Gerritsen, are you familiar with the provisions of the Geneva Convention?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I think you may even have lectured on the issue; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And does the Geneva Convention apply to most armies?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They must do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did the Geneva Convention apply to the HVO?
